title: Hamsa, the mantra in every breath
hookLine: a yoga Upanishad hears hamsa in every breath, and teachers turn it into so'ham: I am That
carry: so'ham: every breath says i am that
tomorrow: why would silent japa count most?

cards: Ha, on the way out. Sa, on the way in. Breathe out slowly through the nose, and the air makes a soft sound, close to an h.
Breathe in, and there's a faint hiss, close to an s. Easy to miss; it's just breath. But some yoga texts heard something more.
To them, that soft sound was a mantra, repeated day and night by every breathing creature, without anyone choosing to say it.

teach.b: The text is the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, one of the yoga Upanishads. In paraphrase: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes back in with the sound sa, and so the living being is always repeating hamsa, hamsa.
This, it says, is called the ajapa gayatri.
Ajapa means not-japa: repetition that happens without effort, with no beads, no lips, no count.

teach.h: THE SWAN THAT TELLS MILK FROM WATER.
teach.b: Hamsa is also the Sanskrit word for a swan or a wild goose, and in Indian poetry the swan can sip the milk out of milk mixed with water.
So it became a picture of a soul that can tell the real from the passing, and the greatest renunciates are given the title paramahamsa, the supreme swan.
Some teachers turn the sound around: so'ham, I am That.

teach.h: THE ATMAN IS NOT SEPARATE FROM BRAHMAN.
teach.b: Vedanta teachers hear in those two syllables one of this path's biggest ideas: the Self in you, the atman, is not finally separate from Brahman, the one reality in everything.
Read that way, every breathing creature says it all day, a sparrow, a grandmother, a baby asleep, and almost nobody hears.
For four days this practice has been about keeping a mantra going: setting terms, counting beads, tying it to dawn and dusk. Ajapa adds something quieter. The repetition isn't only the one you push.
It's also the one you finally hear. Some teachers keep the beads and the chosen mantra and let it ride on the breath, one part on the out-breath, one on the in. The discipline stays.
It just rides on a sound that was already saying who you are.

how: Some Hindu yoga teachers teach ajapa japa, listening to the breath's own sound as hamsa or so'ham, often read as 'I am That', and letting a chosen mantra move with the in-breath and out-breath.

o: a mantra kept daily, riding the breath's own sound
a mantra shouted loudly to drown out the breath
a single long breath held while chanting once

games.q: the mantra in the breath — tap the pairs.
p: japa not done, the effortless one
the supreme swan, a title for great sages

s: ajapa japa means skipping your mantra practice
it means the repetition that happens without effort, the breath's own hamsa.
the Dhyanabindu Upanishad hears ha in the out-breath and sa in the in-breath
it says the living being is always repeating hamsa, and calls this the ajapa gayatri.
Vedanta teachers read so'ham as 'I am That'
they hear in it the teaching that the atman, the Self, is not finally separate from Brahman.

games.q: your little cousin hears that the breath is 'saying a mantra.' what is it saying, in this teaching?
o: hamsa, or turned around, so'ham: I am That.
how many breaths you have left.
games.why: the Dhyanabindu hears ha out and sa in: hamsa. many teachers turn it to so'ham, I am That, and read it as the atman one with Brahman.

practice: Let the breath move through the nose, no counting, and listen: a soft ha on the out-breath, a faint sa on the in, not made any louder.

If you've been keeping a mantra, let it rest on that sound, part on the out-breath and part on the in; if not, stay with hamsa, or with the breath's own sound. When the mind drifts, come back to listening.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, hamsa, so'ham, I am That.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: ajapa, japa not done, the mantra the breath repeats by itself.

carryVoice: Your line: so'ham, every breath says I am That. The atman and Brahman, in two syllables. I'll be here tomorrow.
